question: What is the main job of a flight nurse?

options.D: Providing medical care during aircraft transport

explanation: You've got this! Flight nurses specialize in looking after patients and giving continuous medical care while flying in an aircraft. Simple and vital!

question: Why do we use air ambulances for patients in remote areas?

options.A: It bridges the gap to advanced medical facilities
options.B: It is always cheaper than ground ambulance transport
options.C: Patients prefer flying over riding in cars
options.D: Hospitals do not accept ground transfers

explanation: Spot on! When patients are far away from big hospitals, air transport moves them quickly so they can get the high-level care they desperately need.

question: During which major conflicts did helicopters first become popular for rapid medical evacuation?
explanation: Great job! Helicopters really changed wartime nursing during the Korean and Vietnam wars, helping nurses reach injured soldiers much closer to the front lines.

question: How has flight nursing changed from the old days to modern times?

options.A: It changed from using airplanes to using boats exclusively
options.B: It stopped focusing on patient stability during flight
options.C: It shifted from basic transport to mobile intensive care
options.D: It moved from caring for civilians to only caring for soldiers

explanation: Exactly! While it used to be mostly about just moving patients from point A to point B, today's flight nurses bring full ICU-level care right up into the skies.

question: Which gas law explains why trapped air inside a patient's body expands as an aircraft climbs?
explanation: Think of Boyle's Law: pressure and volume are opposites! When cabin pressure drops at high altitudes, trapped body gases expand. You'll master this physics connection in no time.

question: Why does flying at high altitudes put patients at risk for low oxygen levels (hypoxia)?

options.A: The barometric pressure drops, reducing available oxygen levels
options.B: Cold cabin temperatures destroy red blood cells
options.C: The aircraft engines consume all the oxygen in the cabin
options.D: Patients stop breathing naturally due to engine noise

explanation: You got it! As you go higher up, atmospheric pressure drops, making it harder for oxygen to pass into the lungs. That's why cabin oxygen monitoring is so crucial.

question: What kind of work background does a nurse usually need before training in flight nursing?

options.A: Certification as an airline commercial pilot
options.B: A degree in mechanical or aerospace engineering
options.C: Experience in intensive care or emergency nursing
options.D: At least five years of experience working in a pharmacy

explanation: Makes sense, right? Caring for unstable patients in mid-air takes tough, seasoned hands—so strong ICU or emergency background is a must-have!

question: Why must flight nurses be great at making quick, independent decisions?

options.A: They operate far away from immediate physician backup
options.B: Flight nurses work completely alone without any crew members
options.C: Pilots are not allowed to talk to medical staff
options.D: Hospitals do not provide guidelines for patient care

explanation: Spot on! Up in the air, you often don't have a doctor standing next to you, so flight nurses must trust their training and act fast.

question: What is a major requirement for medical equipment used inside an aircraft?

options.A: It must be lightweight and battery-operated
options.B: It must be made entirely of glass and porcelain
options.C: It must be larger than standard hospital monitors
options.D: It must plug directly into standard wall sockets

explanation: Brilliant! Space and power are limited in aircraft, so all gear has to be portable, light, and run smoothly on reliable batteries.

question: Why can regular hospital IV pumps sometimes cause trouble during a flight?

options.A: Air pressure causes the IV tubing to melt
options.B: Vibration and pressure changes can affect pump accuracy
options.C: Infusion pumps require constant connection to plumbing
options.D: Hospital pumps are too quiet to hear over the engines

explanation: You're doing great! Engine vibrations and shifts in cabin air pressure can mess with standard pumps, so flight nurses use specially calibrated equipment.

question: What is the main goal of checking a patient (triage) before an air flight?

options.A: Calculating the exact cost of the ambulance fuel
options.B: Choosing which pilot will fly the aircraft
options.D: Determining if the patient can tolerate flight stressors

explanation: Exactly right! We always check if a patient's body can safely handle altitude changes and motion before letting them board.

question: A patient with an untreated collapsed lung (pneumothorax) is booked for a flight. What should be done first?

options.A: Decompress or treat the condition before takeoff
options.B: Fly at a much higher altitude to cure the air pocket
options.C: Remove all supplemental oxygen from the patient
options.D: Proceed with immediate takeoff without any changes

explanation: You nailed it! Remember Boyle's law? Trapped air expands as you go higher, so a pneumothorax must be treated *before* takeoff to prevent a life-threatening crisis.

question: Why is it so hard to listen to breath sounds with a regular stethoscope inside a flying aircraft?

options.A: Flight nurses are not permitted to use stethoscopes
options.B: Air pressure changes destroy the rubber tubing instantly
options.C: Patients stop breathing entirely when the engine starts
options.D: The high level of ambient engine noise masks lung sounds

explanation: Correct! Aircraft engines are very loud. Because the background noise makes auscultation tough, flight nurses rely heavily on monitors and capnography.

question: What is a top clinical priority when caring for a patient mid-flight?

options.B: Maintaining airway security and hemodynamic stability
options.C: Serving meals and beverages to the transport crew

explanation: Spot on, nurse! Keeping the airway clear and vital signs stable will always be your number one duty in any critical transport.

question: In aeromedical work, what does the safety acronym 'CRM' stand for?
explanation: You've got this! CRM is a fantastic aviation safety framework that encourages teamwork, clear communication, and shared problem-solving among everyone on board.

question: Why is Crew Resource Management (CRM) so helpful for flight nurses?

options.A: It replaces the need for medical equipment maintenance
options.B: It empowers any crew member to speak up about safety hazards
options.C: It ensures pilots make all medical decisions alone
options.D: It dictates the exact medications nurses can give in flight

explanation: Brilliant! CRM makes sure that titles don't block safety. If a nurse or paramedic spots a hazard, they can speak up immediately without fear.

question: What makes writing patient notes (charting) tricky for flight nurses during a journey?

options.A: A complete lack of paper and pens in the cabin
options.C: Patients refusing to share their medical history
options.D: Strict laws forbidding written notes in aircraft

explanation: Right on! Trying to write neat, legible notes while the aircraft is shaking and bumping from turbulence is definitely a challenge.

question: Why is keeping clear records of vital signs and treatments especially crucial in flight nursing?

options.A: Insurance companies only pay if notes are written in ink
options.B: It provides a clear record of care despite changing jurisdictions
options.C: Pilots require nursing notes to navigate the aircraft
options.D: It replaces the need for verbal handoffs at the receiving hospital

explanation: You got it! Because air transport often crosses different regions and hospitals, detailed notes ensure smooth handovers and safe, continuous care.
